summary: The Transformer sizing calculator turns the load voltage (V), the minimum kVA required and the spare capacity into load current (I) (Single phase). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Transformer sizing calculator work?
sections.html:
The Transformer sizing calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports load current (I) (Single phase) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select transformer type); then you type in the load voltage (V) (Single phase), the minimum kVA required (Single phase), the spare capacity (Including spare capacity) and the spare capacity (Including spare capacity).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Transformer sizing calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Load current (I)=1000 × minimum kVA required ÷ load voltage (V)
Load voltage (V)=(1000 ÷ 3) × the square root of (3) × minimum kVA required ÷ load current (I)
KVA with spare capacity=(1 ÷ 100) × minimum kVA required × (spare capacity + 100)
Single suggested size=(minimum kVA required, 0)
Single spare size=(KVA with spare capacity, 0)
Minimum kVA required=100 × KVA with spare capacity ÷ (spare capacity + 100)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Select transformer type set to Single-phase, Load voltage (V) = 10 V, Minimum kVA required = 10 and Spare capacity = 20. Working through the relationship above gives Load current (I) = 1000 A and kVA with spare capacity = 12.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Load current (I) = 1000 A and kVA with spare capacity = 12 should be roughly the size you expected from Select transformer type set to Single-phase and Load voltage (V) = 10 V.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Transformer sizing calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the load voltage (V), the minimum kVA required and the spare capacity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Transformer sizing calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns load current (I) (Single phase), derived from the load voltage (V), the minimum kVA required and the spare capacity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Transformer sizing calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the load voltage (V), the minimum kVA required and the spare capacity, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter load current (I) (Single phase) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Load current (I) (Single phase) opens in amperes and the chip beside it offers 3 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Load current (I) = 1000 A. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Transformer sizing calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
